rationale: The book's identification of 'heart of the earth' as Jerusalem requires a multi-step symbolic chain (earth = land; heart = center via navel/midst in Ezek; mirror to bilvav yammim; sea = nations) plus redefinition of Jonah 2 language (mountains = kingdoms; fish = ruler) to force a full Passion typology and a non-burial start for the three days. The strongest counter needs far fewer steps: Jesus' explicit parallel equates the fish-belly confinement with the Son of Man's confinement, and Jonah himself already labels that confinement Sheol plus 'the earth with her bars.' That reading accounts for the primary comparison, the death-burial-resurrection core of the sign, and the shared 'earth' vocabulary without inventing new dictionary entries or shifting the 'as...so' terms. The chronology problem is real but is more economically handled by Hebrew inclusive reckoning than by relocating the referent. Because the counter better explains the same texts with smaller unsupported moves, and because Jonah 2:6 is a detail the Jerusalem core cannot absorb without contradiction or redefinition, the common interpretation prevails.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem as the navel and heart of the land (the city God set in the midst of the nations)
book_secondary_elaborations: Entire Jonah narrative as scene-by-scene prophecy of betrayal, trial, death, resurrection and turn to the nations
Great fish as devouring ruler (Caesar/Rome) and kingdom
Three days and three nights counted from arrest in Jerusalem rather than from burial
Mountains as kingdoms so that 'bottoms of the mountains' and 'earth with her bars' mean subjection under the world-powers
Sea as peoples/nations so that 'heart of the seas' mirrors 'heart of the earth'
strongest_counter_interpretation: The tomb or the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades) during the interval between Jesus' death and resurrection, the direct antitype of Jonah's three days and nights in the fish's belly which Jonah himself calls the belly of Sheol and the earth with bars
counter_core_identification: The grave/tomb or underworld place of the dead
material_core_denial: Denies that the phrase denotes Jerusalem (or the land's geographic center) rather than the place of burial and sojourn among the dead
counter_case: Matthew 12:40 constructs a strict parallel: duration 'in the whale's belly' = duration 'in the heart of the earth'; the location being compared is therefore the place of confinement, not a city.
Jonah 2:2 and 2:6 already interpret the fish experience as 'the belly of Sheol' and 'the earth with her bars was about me,' supplying the exact conceptual and lexical bridge for 'heart of the earth.'

The sign is repeatedly linked in the NT to death, burial and third-day resurrection (1 Cor 15:3-4; Acts 2:24-31 with Ps 16:10; the 'lower parts of the earth' in Eph 4:9), not to time spent inside a city.
No OT text ever calls Jerusalem 'the heart of the earth'; Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12 use 'midst' and 'navel of the land,' so the identification needs extra symbolic and external scaffolding.
The traditional reading requires only the face-value comparison plus Jonah's own prayer language; it does not depend on later-defined symbols for sea, fish, mountain or navel.
book_explanatory_advantages: Avoids the well-known Friday-to-Sunday counting tension by starting the three days and nights at the arrest inside Jerusalem (cf. Luke 24:21).
Uses a consistent OT-search method and the mirror phrase 'heart of the seas' to give 'heart of the earth' an intra-biblical location.
Explains why Jesus offered the whole of Jonah (Luke 11:30) rather than a single chronological clause, generating many Passion correspondences.
Correctly notes that no verse of Scripture ever labels a tomb 'the heart of the earth.'
counter_explanatory_advantages: Rests on the explicit 'as...so' syntax of Matthew 12:40 and on Jonah's self-description of the same three-day location.
Needs no auxiliary dictionary (sea = nations, fish = king, mountain = kingdom, earth = land-center) to reach its referent.

Aligns with the physical fact that Jesus' body lay in a rock-hewn tomb in the earth for the relevant interval and with the earliest Christian summary 'buried... raised the third day according to the scriptures.'
Accounts for the Sheol/Hades language that appears both in Jonah's prayer and in the apostolic preaching of the resurrection.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Jonah 2:6 ('the earth with her bars was about me for ever') is spoken of the very place and duration that Jesus equates with 'the heart of the earth'; the Jerusalem reading must either ignore this shared 'earth' vocabulary or redefine 'earth' in two incompatible senses within the same sign, producing a contradiction with the parallel structure of Matthew 12:40.
unresolved_objections: The precise reckoning of 'three days and three nights' under a Friday crucifixion remains awkward for the tomb reading and has generated alternative calendars.
Several of the book's scene-by-scene parallels (lots, innocent blood, first Gentile confession, anger at Gentile mercy) are genuinely striking and are not required by the narrow tomb interpretation.
Extra-biblical Jewish and early Christian sources do call Jerusalem the navel or heart of the earth, giving the minority reading some historical pedigree.
